apx-pack: Backs slide 6, which says the lender view is part of this round’s build. The page shows what that view is for: five decisions a lender makes on a funded project, what each is made on today and what IRIS adds. Funds left to finish: lenders call this keeping the loan in balance, cost to complete against undrawn funds and equity. The QS assesses cost to complete on the footing that the original builder finishes for the contract price (AIQS guidance note, 2019); IRIS adds the builder’s own forecast and what is moving it, such as variations not yet priced, delays not yet notified and trades let against allowances. Completion date: presale settlements repay the loan, and completion past a sunset date lets purchasers rescind. Notices matter because entitlement to time and money depends on notices given in time; a missed notice turns a recoverable delay into the builder’s own cost. Builder failure: what the lender recovers is roughly the completed value, less the cost to finish and the cost of delay; the assessment service is on A9. Scope: IRIS reads the funded project and makes no solvency call on the builder as a company. A builder short of cash tends to show it on the project first, as trades paid late or packages left unlet. Status: planned capability. The design-partner lender decides what the view shows and how it is laid out; the milestone is IRIS for Lenders on a live facility beside the lender’s QS at month 9 (slide 13). Each line on the view links to the source records behind it, and a pack can be exported at each drawdown to sit beside the QS report.
apx-mechanism: Backs slide 4, which shows three lines of the lender’s QS report and what sits beneath each. This page gives all six causes, grouped under the same three lines. The report: a lender’s QS progress drawdown report typically carries a development cost table, work in place valued against the builder’s claim, programme and extensions of time, cost to complete, variations as submitted, approvals, insurances, the builder’s statutory declaration that subcontractors are paid, risk items and a cash flow forecast. The AIQS guidance note (Construction Financing Reports, 2nd edition, 2019) has the QS assess cost to complete on the footing that the original contractor completes the works. Reports commonly state that information supplied was not independently verified. The six causes. 1. Time bars: delay notices, variations, latent conditions and provisional-sum adjustments each carry a notice period; what is near or past its bar decides whether a cost is recoverable or the builder’s own, with liquidated damages on top. 2. Completion: labour on site against the programme, and open defects and rework against practical completion, show whether the date will be reached. 3. Cost not yet notified: the records show delays and changes coming before a notice is lodged, and each carries consequential cost, most visibly preliminaries that extend with the delay. 4. Soft forecast: much of a forecast final cost sits as contingency inside trade budgets and as allowances; how much is still soft is a risk measure in itself. 5. Trades still to let: rates fixed at tender are open to the market once labour and material prices move; scope still to let, or let against an allowance, is price risk still open. 6. Trades paid: with each claim the builder declares that its subcontractors have been paid what is owed (in Queensland, a supporting statement under section 75 of the BIF Act); the payment records show each trade’s claims, approvals and payments. ASIC found false declarations may signal cash flow problems (16-325MR, 2016). Basis: the report column from the AIQS guidance; the causes from the founders’ work inside builders.
apx-since-2021: Backs slide 4’s closing line: since 2021, fixed prices, thinner builders and a trend of in-house delivery have moved more of the risk inside the project. Fixed prices: Probuild, Condev, PBS, Porter Davis, St Hilliers and Roberts Co failed between 2022 and 2025 (reported; the timeline is on slide 3). Thinner builders: construction was 26.1% of companies entering external administration in FY2022, 27.9% in FY2023, 26.9% in FY2024, 24.4% in FY2025 and 24.5% in FY2025-26 (ASIC series 1, 14 September 2026). In-house delivery: where builder and developer are related entities or co-investors, the builder’s margin and the developer’s equity are the same group capital, so a project loss has no second balance sheet to land on and the builder tends to fail with the developer. Bathla’s in-house builder entered administration with the group on 25 August 2026. The share of jobs delivered in-house or by joint venture is a founder observation and has not been measured. Under the builder’s side deed a lender can take the developer’s place if the developer defaults; where the builder has failed too, lenders appoint receivers and fund a replacement builder. Presales: Stamford Capital’s Real Estate Debt Capital Markets Survey, run in March and April 2026, found 37% of construction lenders requiring no presales, up from 29% in 2025 and 18% in 2023, while the share requiring 60 to 100% presales fell from about 45% in 2021 to 8%. Lending has tightened since August 2026 (slide 8). Many jobs still run at arm’s length on a fixed price; the four changes are observed developments, with sources on A7.
apx-reach: Backs slide 10. Why each party signs. The lender lends against cost to finish and the completion date, and today reads both from the QS report and the builder’s own report each month; IRIS gives it the same figures from the records as they move, with the record behind each one. That a lender values this enough to write it into a facility is the hypothesis the design partner tests. The developer already pays for lender-required monitoring, the QS report, as a condition of its debt; IRIS is paid the same way, at 15 bps a year. That a lender prices a facility it can see into at a lower rate is a hypothesis put to the design partner (D-46); no lender has confirmed it. The builder: on a facility with the condition, IRIS is a condition of the tender for all bidders, so no bidder is put at a disadvantage, and the builder sees each finding before the lender does. Whether builders accept it is untested until a lender adopts. What binds whom. The facility agreement binds the borrower, as a condition of drawdown. The builder is bound by what it signs: the tender and award conditions, a head contract clause giving read-only API access to that project’s systems for monitoring, and the side deed (tripartite deed) signed by lender, developer and builder at financial close, which lenders already require. A builder already under contract owes nothing new; the first conditions go on new facilities, extensions and refinances. The builder’s duty stands on its own and is not a precondition to its payment claims: a contractual precondition to payment claims was held void in BRB Modular v AWX [2015] QSC 218. The drawdown condition is met by an exported pack, so a builder cannot hold up the developer’s drawdown. Where interests pull apart, and how IRIS handles it. Lender and builder: the lender wants detail; the builder wants its margin and trade prices kept. Proposed rule (O-20): the lender and developer see totals, movement and the records behind them; trade letting and rates stay in the builder’s view unless cost to finish exceeds what is left in the contract, or the lender steps in under its deed. Subcontract confidentiality terms decide what trade data can be shown. Developer and lender: the developer pays and the lender relies. IRIS is paid a fixed fee per facility with no share of any outcome; it reports what the builder’s system of record shows, and where the builder’s internal and developer-facing forecasts differ it reports the system of record and flags the gap without adjudicating. Builder first (proposed; not yet in the product requirements, O-21): the builder sees each finding first and can add its explanation before the lender view refreshes; the finding and the explanation then reach the lender together, and the history is kept. One job, one fee: a job under a lender’s condition pays the facility fee, and the builder’s subscription applies to its other jobs. Assessments are a fixed fee per engagement, with no stake in the recovery. Reliance and data permissions are on A13. The drafting is confirmed with lawyers at the month-9 opinion; this is not legal advice.
apx-sizing: Backs the three market figures on slide 11. Each step is a line on the workbook’s Market sheet, and each input is on the Inputs sheet with its source and type, so the chain can be rebuilt from the published figures. 1. Building work a year in scope: apartment work, medium-rise $18.9bn plus high-rise $14.6bn (IBISWorld E3019, 2025-26), plus commercial and industrial building of $70.9bn (IBISWorld E3021, 2026-27) × 65% on jobs of $10M or more, a company estimate because IBISWorld does not split by job size: $33.5bn + $46.1bn = $79.6bn. 2. Value under construction at one time = work a year × build time: apartments 29 months (ABS average completion time, 2025-26), commercial 24 months (estimate; ABS non-residential work yet to be done was $76.4bn in March 2026 against about $70bn a year): $81.0bn + $92.2bn = $173.1bn. 3. With a construction facility: developers fund 88% of apartment and 73.1% of commercial work (IBISWorld major markets): $138.6bn. 4. Live jobs = value ÷ a $40M market average contract: 4,328, of which 3,465 carry a facility and 863 do not. Cross-checks on the $40M: a listed lender’s senior construction loans average about $39M (June 2026); Brisbane and Gold Coast apartment jobs on hold average about $48M (PRD, September 2026); the top 50 builders’ 2025 starts averaged about $61M (Hubexo, April 2026). 5. TAM: each live job is priced once. A job with a facility pays 15 bps on the market’s average facility, $40M × 1.2 = $48M, which is $72,000 a year; a job without one pays the builder subscription, $3,500 a month or $42,000 a year; assessments add 4% of funded jobs a year × $35,000 = $4.9M. TAM = 3,465 × $72,000 + 863 × $42,000 + $4.9M = $290.6M. 6. SAM: the jobs with a construction facility, where a lender can set the condition: $249.5M of facility fees plus $4.9M of assessments = $254.4M (D-54). It leaves out the $36.2M of subscriptions on jobs with no facility, which the plan reaches builder by builder. Queensland, where the first builders are, is the first market: 816 live jobs and $54.9M priced the same way; South East Queensland is about 79% of the state’s pipeline (CSQ). 7. SOM: the base case’s run rate at month 60, 373 facilities × $120,000 + 92 builder jobs × $42,000 + assessments = $49.2M, 19% of SAM and 17% of TAM. SOM is counted the same way as TAM, live jobs at one moment × their annual price, which is why it uses the month-60 run rate; Year 5 revenue, the sum of months 49 to 60, is $40.5M (A6). Checks: the 465 jobs under IRIS at month 60 are 11% of live jobs; the 373 facilities at $80M are $29.8bn, 18% of the $166bn of construction facility value ($138.6bn × 1.2). Three sizes: $40M counts the jobs in the market; $48M is the market’s average facility and prices the market; $80M is the average facility the plan’s lenders put under IRIS (D-50), larger because the lenders that adopt first write the mid- and high-rise jobs. It sets the lender revenue line and leaves the market unchanged (D-52). Out of scope: low-rise apartments, townhouses and houses, mostly jobs under $10M, and public work, which carries no construction facility. Insurers and surety providers are not counted. The $40M average and the 65% share move the market most; both are estimates.
apx-model: Backs the base case on slide 11. The workbook runs five years in three cases; each row on this page is on its Inputs or Summary sheet. Lender acquisition: lenders adopt at months 12, 18, 22, 26, 29, 32, 34 and 36, then about six a year to 20 at month 60, a company target. Lender 1 is the design partner; lenders 2 onwards follow a live result there. The market is concentrated: real estate private credit in Australia is about $80bn, 31% of residential development debt, and the five largest providers hold 52% of it (CBRE, 15 November 2026), so a handful of adoptions carries most of the volume. The number of active construction lenders is not published. Facility conversion: each lender adds 0.8 new facilities a month, about ten a year, which at $80M is about $770M of new construction facilities a year, a book of about $1.5bn on two-year terms; plus ten existing loans re-signed under the condition over 18 months at extension or refinance; facilities leave after a 24-month term. The Year 5 book is $29.8bn of facility limits across twenty lenders, which assumes the larger lenders adopt first; the test is the design partner’s own origination. Pricing: 15 bps a year on the facility limit, $120,000 on $80M, above a $3,500 a month floor with no cap (D-51). For scale, non-bank senior construction facilities were priced in the high single digits to low double digits a year in 2026, with establishment and line fees of one to a few per cent of the limit (Feasly, July 2026); 15 bps is about 1.5% of a year’s interest at 10%. No lender has agreed the fee; the design partner is asked what it would pay. Retention: no lender stops adding facilities within five years (an input, D-55). A facility under the condition keeps it to completion; a lender that leaves adds no new ones. If each lender stopped after three years, Year 5 revenue would fall by $1.0M; each mature lender is about $2.2M a year of fees (about 19 facilities). Unit economics in Year 5 terms: one facility pays $120,000 a year; a deployment analyst at one per eight live jobs costs about $16,800 a job, cloud and model use $3,000, and commission (8% of the first year’s fee) with onboarding ($4,000) spread over the term $6,800; contribution $93,400, 78%. A builder job pays $42,000 and carries the same analyst and cloud cost. Operating margin, Year 5: revenue $40.5M; costs that grow with jobs $10.7M; lender success and engineering $4.3M; fixed costs (directors, fixed roles, overheads, contingency) $7.4M; EBITDA $18.1M, 45%. The analyst ratio is the largest cost lever: six jobs each takes Year 5 EBITDA to $15.8M. Revenue and run rate: Year 5 revenue is the sum of months 49 to 60. Revenue grows through the year, from $2.6M in month 49 to $4.1M in month 60, so the run rate (month × 12) is $31.8M at month 49 and $49.2M at month 60. Builder line: two pilots pay from month 6, then a new builder at intervals of four to eight months, each starting with two jobs and growing to six, at $3,500 a month a job. Assessments: from month 30, $35,000 each, benchmarked to QS report fees. Results: revenue $0.19M / $2.3M / $9.3M / $22.7M / $40.5M; EBITDA −$0.48M / −$0.31M / $2.4M / $8.9M / $18.1M; upside $78M and conservative $6.2M in Year 5. Downside cases on A15.
apx-sources: Backs the dated figures on slides 2, 3 and 8. Sources are linked where the address names no lender or fund; the full register, with each address, is research/source-register.md. Exposure and loss: a sum owed to lenders is exposure, money lent and at risk; losses are set as receivers sell and funds revalue. The losses recognised so far are write-downs: three listed credit funds wrote down about $168M, 4.7% of their combined net assets, before trading was halted on 28 September 2026 (The Urban Developer, 30 September 2026); quotation was reinstated in October (CFS notice, 7 October 2026). One lender’s senior Bathla loan was sold for about $31.2M and a receiver appointed to settle presales (ABC News, 17 October 2026). Construction insolvencies: ASIC insolvency statistics, series 1, published 14 September 2026: 3,472 of 14,153 companies entering external administration in FY2025-26, 24.5%; 37.4% in July and August 2026 with the Bathla entities and 23.5% without (via The Good Builder, 22 September 2026). Bathla: 540 entities into administration on 25 August 2026 (ASIC data, via The Good Builder); about A$3.3bn owed (AFR; others report $3.4bn) and about 40 funds exposed (Bloomberg), both as reported by Alternative Credit Investor, 1 October 2026; about $3.08bn owed to secured lenders within about $3.4bn of total creditor debt, sites closed and receivers appointed (administrator’s updates, The Urban Developer, 25 September 2026). Slide 3: a lender of about ten years exited its exposure by January 2026, refinancing its remaining projects to about 12 other lenders from late 2024 (The Urban Developer, 25 August 2026); the group entered administration seven months later. A rating of one project shown on an earlier version of slide 3 was not found in open sources and has been taken off (O-25). Rates and housing: RBA cash rate to 4.85% on 3 November 2026 after five rises from 3.60% (RBA media release 26-30); ABS monthly CPI, 4.9% to October, published 25 November 2026; Cotality national index for October, published 2 November 2026, 6.7% below the March peak. Regulation: ASIC REP 814, 820 and 823 (2025); the 52-fund review of $76bn before 30 June 2026 and the Commissioner’s warning of 22 September (Clayton Utz, 1 October 2026); ASIC’s statement of 30 September naming residential construction (The Nightly, 30 September 2026). Valuation: on 18 June 2026 ASIC told private credit funds to refresh 30 June valuations and not to wait for a formal default before reassessing values; FSC Standard No. 30, Private Markets Best Practice Principles, issued 26 August 2026 and in force from 1 July 2027, requires valuation policies with independence and effective challenge, and its guidance note puts good practice at valuing at least quarterly in most circumstances. Lending terms: Stamford Capital Real Estate Debt Capital Markets Survey 2026 (March and April 2026); Gravity Capital Australian Private Credit Index, September quarter 2026, published 25 October 2026. Founder experience, labelled as such: the replacement-builder premium of 20 to 40%, and the three project examples on slide 5, which come from private records with figures altered so the jobs cannot be identified. Market and model inputs are on A5 and A6; competitor sources on A8.
apx-landscape: Backs slide 9. About sixty products and firms were reviewed in October 2026 across eight categories, with four Australian entrants added on 4 November (Korrix, Cintech, Vyne and SteelCap, which is a landing page) and the lender-side and Australian builder-side sites re-read on 26 November 2026: builder project-management platforms (Procore, Oracle Aconex, Autodesk Construction Cloud, Trimble Viewpoint, CMiC, Buildertrend, Fieldwire); builder ERP and cost systems (Jobpac, Cheops, Workbench, Premier, Buildxact, Simpro, Lentune); trade payment and compliance (Payapps, IPEX, Earlytrade, Textura, GCPay, Queensland project trust accounts); lender-side draw and monitoring tools (Built, Rabbet, Land Gorilla, Northspyre, nCino, Abrigo); owner project controls (Mastt, Kahua, InEight, Primavera, Asite, Aphex); AI on construction records (Datagrid, Document Crunch, Trunk Tools, Alloovium, Octant, Slate, nPlan, Buildots, Doxel, OpenSpace, ALICE, Briq); credit and counterparty data (CreditorWatch, Equifax iCIRT, illion, Dun and Bradstreet); and the service incumbents (the lender’s QS firms; KordaMentha, McGrathNicol, FTI, Deloitte, KPMG). Three questions were asked of each: does it reconcile across source systems; does it give the lender a project-level position; is it written into facility documents. The lender’s QS report meets the third as established practice; IPEX’s vendor claims the third for some lenders; Built, Rabbet and Land Gorilla are required operationally by US lenders, with no facility wording found, and Built reads Procore financials at the head-contract draw level. Cross-system reconciliation exists builder-side (Datagrid, Slate, Trunk Tools, Alloovium, Briq) and lender-side on submitted packages (Built); none found combines both and reports outward to builder, developer and lender. Limits: public sources; in-house tools at Tier 1 builders or lenders cannot be seen; IPEX’s own site was not readable in the review session, so its material is as reported in sponsored articles. We would consider a partnership with a product close enough in logic to merge with. The dated sources are in the repository’s research register.
apx-recovery: Backs the references to distressed-project assessments on slides 2, 3, 6, 10 and 11. Proposed and not yet demonstrated: the platform is proven on builder pilots and shaped with a lender design partner first; assessments are offered as part of scaling, at a separate fee per engagement, because distress is where the information problem is most expensive and where a lender already pays outside advisers. The first assessment is a controlled one on a historic record set, scored against the outcome reached, before any live engagement. Fee: fixed per engagement and no share of the recovery, so IRIS has no stake in what it reports; $35,000 in the model, benchmarked to QS report fees; about 14 engagements in Year 5, about 2% of revenue. What it gives: where the project stands across the delivery domains, each finding valued, dated and linked to its record, and a register of gaps. An incoming builder will not take liability for the failed builder’s work, so it prices what it cannot see; a position traced to the records, with gaps listed, narrows what it has to price blind. Speed: a first position in days from access is the design aim; it depends on how complete the records are. Access: before an appointment, the facility’s information rights and the builder’s side deed; after one, a receiver appointed over the developer takes the developer’s rights under the head contract and can give consent, and if the builder is in administration its administrator controls its books and software subscriptions, so access needs the administrator’s agreement. The strongest case is IRIS on the project before a failure. What stays with others: the QS, the valuer and the insolvency practitioner; IRIS does not advise on the decision, value the asset, certify cost to complete or assess the builder’s solvency. The legal pathway is confirmed with lawyers at the month-9 opinion; not legal advice.
apx-risks: Backs the milestones on slide 13. Each question is one an investor would ask before the seed, and the round is built to answer them in this order. 1. Live data, month 6: the first release of the platform plan (pilot proof) running on the R&D partner’s jobs and judged against the pass marks on A14. The R&D partnership is agreed; its agreement and data terms are being finalised. 2. Paying builders, month 6: the model has two builders paying from month 6; the R&D partner uses IRIS without a fee. 3. Security, month 6: an independent security audit and penetration test, with the access review and the questionnaire pack lenders send; certification to a standard follows when a lender’s procurement requires it (A13). 4. A lender using it, month 9: the design partner runs a scoped lender view beside its QS on one live facility. The platform plan places full lender and developer views in its seventh release, so month 9 depends on a scoped view being brought forward on the first release’s data and access controls; to be confirmed with the technical lead. 5. The documents, month 9: a legal opinion on the drawdown condition, the tender condition, the head contract clause and the side deed (A4). 6. The condition, month 12: the first drawdown condition with the design partner, a company target. 7. Fundability, months 15 to 18: the seed is raised on paid builder use, with or without the condition; at the plan’s spend it is needed by month 19 (A15). Other risks. Competition: platforms report to their own customer, and requiring one would dictate the builder’s software; QS and restructuring firms could add the capability and are as likely to be channels as rivals; Procore with Datagrid is the platform to watch (slide 9). Sales cycles: lender procurement, panels and legal review are slow; lenders a year late take Year 5 revenue to $24M with cash still positive (A15). Connections: builder-authorised API connections, one adapter per system, built system by system, Procore first. Assessments: access after an appointment, and pricing, which is a fixed fee so that IRIS has no stake in the recovery (A9).
apx-status: Backs the status line on slide 2. Built: the proof of concept on a populated Procore sandbox: a fictional project with constructed records, reconciled into positions across six domains, with findings that open to their records and a chat prototype. It has not been connected to a live project and no accuracy figure is claimed for it (slide 7). Agreed: an R&D partnership with a South East Queensland Tier 2 builder, giving access to real project data in return for the use of IRIS on its projects; the agreement and its data-processing terms are being finalised. In negotiation: an engineering partner to build the enterprise product; the statement of work is being prepared, and the $320K build line in the use of funds is an allowance until the partner’s quote. Feedback in writing: at an advisor’s request, a senior contracts manager at a Tier 1 builder reviewed the product summary in May 2026. He named three uses he would value: finding risk in correspondence, subcontractor claims and payment applications; identifying costs the budget or client revenue does not cover, which today depend on a contract administrator recording them by hand, so that a missed one leaves exposure outside the accounting system that senior management does not see; and finding delay events across the project systems that need a notice before a time bar applies, then prompting the extension-of-time notices that follow. His view was conditional on the product doing what it sets out to do. The second and third are pass marks on A14. In discussion: a non-bank private credit fund has said the lender view would be useful to it (founder-reported, D-36); there is no letter or commitment. Targets: two paying builders from month 6; IRIS for Lenders on a live facility at month 9; the first drawdown condition at month 12. Not claimed: paying customers, a lender mandate, completed assessments, an accuracy figure or a security certificate.
apx-architecture: Backs slides 6 and 7. The platform plan (draft for review, November 2026) sets seven constraints: read-only access to the source systems; lineage from each figure to its source record; findings produced by deterministic rules, with models used to classify, extract and explain; tenant isolation by row-level security, tested; contract mechanics such as notice periods and time bars held as data; a canonical project model independent of any vendor’s schema; and retained content encrypted, access-logged and deleted on exit. Layers: source records are landed as received, mapped into the canonical project model, and checked by the verification engine, which writes findings, findings of absence (what should exist and does not) and the links to the evidence; the views and reports read from there. The engine holds its checks as data, gives each finding a stable identity from one run to the next, records the version of the check that produced it, and counts each exposure once in a headline figure. Hosting: Microsoft Azure, Australia East. Today the proof of concept runs on prototype infrastructure against a Procore sandbox; its chat is a demonstration. Each release is anchored to a business milestone: R1 pilot proof, in progress (contract position, programme position, and cost and cash flow on live data; verification checks; evidence drill to source; sign-in and deployment); R2 enterprise foundation (tenant isolation, role-based access, orchestration, point-in-time history, data-quality testing, self-serve onboarding, certification readiness); R3 unstructured intelligence (email and file stores read into the model, with document-derived facts kept as a distinct class of evidence); R4 conversational intelligence (answers that cite records and decline when the data cannot support an answer); R5 multi-source connectors (Aconex, ProcurePro and PayApps, with entity resolution, which completes reconciliation across systems); R6 full domain coverage (trade letting, design and documentation, quality); R7 portfolio and capital layer (scoped developer and funder views with an enforced, auditable boundary). Jobpac is not yet scheduled (O-23). Which releases this round funds is set by the engineering partner’s statement of work. The moat: the canonical model and the library of checks, which encode contract mechanics and grow with each job and each standard form of contract; an evidence trail a lender can audit; and, once the condition is in a lender’s documents, the cost to that lender of changing a monitoring standard written into its facilities. Across enough facilities, the record of findings against outcomes becomes a measure of construction risk that no single builder or lender holds. Not claimed: universal coverage, an accuracy figure, or certification.
apx-security: Backs slides 6 and 10. From the security and privacy section of the platform plan (draft for review, November 2026). Hosting in Microsoft Azure, Australia East; data classified, collected to the minimum the checks need, and encrypted in transit and at rest. Access: the builder authorises each connection, per project, read-only; nothing is written back. Sign-in is by invitation with email and password in the first release, and single sign-on with multi-factor authentication in the second. Authorisation is by organisation and project in the first release, by domain in the second and by record in the seventh, enforced twice: by row-level security in the database and by a filter in the interface. Who sees what (proposed rule, O-20): the builder sees all of its own data; a lender or developer sees the job it funds, as totals, movement and the records behind them, with trade letting and rates kept in the builder’s view unless cost to finish exceeds what is left in the contract or the lender steps in. Auditability: each access to data is logged from the first release; each finding records the version of the check that produced it and links to its source records, and the history is kept, so a lender can see what was known and when. Data handling: the builder is the controller and IRIS the processor; no customer’s data is used for another without permission; a data-processing agreement is signed before any live deployment; retention is set with counsel; on exit the data is deleted and a deletion certificate issued. Assurance: an independent security audit, penetration test and access review, with the questionnaire pack lenders send, in the months after the raise; certification-ready at the second release; formal certification (ISO 27001 or SOC 2) when a lender’s procurement requires it; incident response in place before the first paid deployment. Reliance: what IRIS gives a lender is the builder’s own records, reconciled, dated and linked to their source. IRIS values nothing, certifies nothing and does not assess cost to complete, so the lender relies on where each figure comes from and keeps its QS, its valuer and its own credit judgement. Terms of use say so and are set with the design partner; there is no reliance letter. Professional indemnity and cyber insurance are in place before the first paid deployment, and grow as lender use grows. Service targets proposed for the enterprise release: 99.5% availability in business hours, recovery within four hours, and no more than a day of data lost.
apx-pilot: Backs slides 7 and 13. Proposed by the company as the pass marks for the R&D pilot, to be agreed with the builder before the pilot starts; none has been measured yet. Agreement to source: forecast final cost, cost to date, committed cost and revenue claimed agree to the builder’s month-end cost report for three months running, with each difference explained (timing, accruals, manual journals). Traceability: each figure and each finding opens the source record it rests on, checked by sample. Precision: at least eight in ten of the findings IRIS raises are confirmed as real by the builder’s commercial team. Recall: at least nine in ten of the items in the builder’s own risk and opportunity register are found; items IRIS finds that the register does not hold are counted separately, as value. Lead time: the median finding appears at least 30 days before it shows in the builder’s monthly cost report or PCG report, measured on the live jobs and back-tested on the three historic record sets on slide 5, where the outcome is known. Time bars: each delay event in the records is flagged before its notice deadline under the contract; this is one of the uses a Tier 1 senior contracts manager named in writing (A11). Commercial value: exposure the project team did not already hold, valued and confirmed by the builder, worth at least ten times the subscription, about $420,000 a job a year; this is his second use, cost the budget does not cover that is recorded by hand or missed. Use: the project team uses IRIS unaided for a full monthly reporting cycle, the exit test of the first release. Conversion: the builder pays from month 6. The lender equivalent follows at month 9: the design partner reads the lender view beside its QS report for three months and records which figures it would use in a drawdown decision. When models start reading documents (R3), extraction accuracy is measured against a held-out set.
apx-downside: Backs slides 11 and 13. Each case re-runs the base model with the change named and everything else as on the Inputs sheet; the results are on the workbook’s Sensitivities sheet. Costs follow the plan as written, so hiring for lenders goes ahead in each case. In practice hiring after the seed waits for lenders, which is why the month cash would fall below zero is shown: it is the month by which that decision has to be made. Lenders twelve months later: the first lender at month 24 and 14 lenders by Year 5; Year 5 revenue $24.1M, EBITDA $7.1M, run rate $31.8M; cash stays positive with the seed at month 15. No lender in five years: builders and off-platform assessments reach $3.4M in Year 5; the plan’s hiring would take cash below zero at month 38, so hiring for lenders would stop before then. Lender retention: if each lender stops adding facilities three years after adopting, Year 5 revenue falls by $1.0M, because live facilities keep the condition to completion. The seed: the base case has $3M at month 15. A $1.5M seed is enough at the plan’s spend. At month 21, cash falls below zero from month 20, so the seed needs to land by month 19, or hiring after month 16 waits for it. With no seed at all, cash falls below zero from month 20 to month 27, at worst $79K, and recovers as lender revenue grows; that rests on lenders arriving on plan. Combined: lenders twelve months late and a $1.5M seed at month 21 take cash below zero from month 19, at worst $1.0M, so the plan would be re-cut before the seed. The single-input changes (facility size, fee, facilities per lender, loans re-signed, term, analyst ratio, director pay) are on the same sheet: each $10M of average facility is about $4.6M of Year 5 revenue, and each basis point of fee about $2.5M.
apx-round: Backs slide 13. Instrument: a simple agreement for future equity (SAFE) for A$750K, converting at the next priced round at a valuation cap of A$4M (owner decision, 24 November 2026, D-39; previously $500K at $5M). Whether the cap is pre- or post-money, any discount, pro rata rights and a most-favoured-nation clause are set in the SAFE itself and are to be confirmed by the company. Use of funds: $320K for the enterprise product build with an engineering partner, an allowance until the partner’s quote against the statement of work; $224K for the two directors at $100K each plus 12% superannuation, full-time from close; $46K for the security audit, cloud and models; $20K sales; $20K legal and IP; $20K contingency and insurance; and a $100K runway reserve held to the seed. Runway: the round covers 13 months of the plan’s costs with no revenue; with the plan’s revenue, cash stays above $261K before the seed. The seed: $3M is assumed at month 15, raised on paid builder use with or without a lender’s condition; at the plan’s spend it needs to land by month 19, or hiring after month 16 waits (A15). What the round retires: whether the reconciliation holds on live data, whether builders pay, whether a lender’s security review passes, whether a lender uses the view beside its QS, and whether the documents hold (A10). Month 9 depends on a scoped lender view being brought forward from the seventh release of the platform plan (A12).
